newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan upbeat on economy but warns on inflation.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan upbeat on economy but warns on inflation.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan Tuesday warned of the risks of higher inflation but gave little indication that the nation's central bank was poised to do anything about it now.
In testimony to Congress that was greeted with relief on Wall Street, Greenspan painted a picture of an economy that showed few signs of faltering after nearly six years of expansion.

"The economy has retained considerable vigour, with few signs of the imbalances and inflationary tensions that have disrupted past expansions," the central bank chief told the Senate Budget Committee.
That was in no small part due to a surprising lack of inflation pressures. But Greenspan made clear that that could not last forever and said the Fed needed to be wary as a result.

In wide-ranging testimony, Greenspan also raised alarms about the long-term health of the Social Security pension system but voiced opposition to Republican calls for a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution.
On Wall Street, stock and bond prices bounded higher after Greenspan's testimony as investors took comfort in his soothing comments.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 40.03 points to 6,883.90, another record, and the 30-year Treasury rose about half a point, lowering its yield to 6.79 percent from 6.83 percent on Friday. The bond market was closed on Monday for the Martin Luther King Jr. holiday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
"The testimony was much more positive than had been anticipated," said Michael LaTronica, director of research at the Wall Street brokerage Gruntal and Co.

Greenspan argued that a big reason for America's good inflation performance was subdued wage demands by workers worried about losing their jobs in a period of corporate downsizing and other structural changes.
But with the labour market "exceptionally tight," it was only a matter of time before workers grew more confident and began pushing for higher pay, he said.

"Indeed, the recent pick-up in some measures of wages suggests that the transition may already be running its course," Greenspan said. "The important question from a monetary policy point of view is whether prospective labour market conditions will be consistent with the maintenance of satisfactory price performance," he said.
He made clear that the central bank was also keeping its eye on the soaring stock market.

Greenspan rocked world financial markets last month when he said the central bank had to be wary when "irrational exuberance" infected stock and other asset prices because that could end up damaging the economy.

The Fed chief did not back away from those remarks on Tuesday. "It was not a shot from the hip," he said. "We thought long and in detail that any such statement could very well have immediate market effects."
But he said he would have preferred that his original remarks were read in their full context.
He called the steep run-up on Wall Street "breathtaking" but said he was encouraged by Americans' increased propensity to invest in mutual funds and other savings vehicles.
He stressed the importance of increased U.S. savings for the economy as a whole. "Attaining a higher national savings rate quite soon is crucial," he said.
To help boost the savings rate, Greenspan urged lawmakers to balance the budget and eventually move it into surplus.
But he said a constitutional amendment was not the way to do that. "I don't like the idea of embodying concrete issues in the Constitution," the long-time Republican said.
President Clinton, who has opposed Republican calls for such an amendment, welcomed Greenspan's remarks.
Greenspan voiced "considerable" concern about the long-term health of the government-run Social Security pension system as the baby-boom generation starts to retire.
The system is expected to go bankrupt in the year 2029, but Greenspan suggested it may happen sooner. "History shows we tend to over-estimate the soundness of the system."

Some experts have advocated allowing the Social Security trust fund to invest in stocks rather than just in low-yielding bonds, to help restore its health. But Greenspan made clear that that alone was not the answer to the system's ills.
